News.title: Man, 24, charged with four counts of rape after two women in their 20s and 40s attacked separately
News.content:
'RAPE' HORROR Man, 24, charged with four counts of rape after two women in their 20s and 40s attacked separately

A MAN has been charged with four counts of rape, after two women in their 20s and 40s were allegedly attacked on separate occasions.

The most recent assault reportedly took place near Chesterfield College, Derbyshire, in the early hours of August 8.

Cops carried out immediate enquiries after the woman, in her 20s, reported the attack.

Dylan Hall was later arrested on August 11 in Chesterfield on suspicion of rape.





He was also arrested in connection with a previous rape which allegedly occurred on June 18 in 2023 in Queen’s Park in Chesterfield.

The woman, in her 40s, reported the alleged attack to the force in March 2026.

Hall, of Park Road, Chesterfield, was charged with four counts of rape on August 12, with one relating to the 2026 incident, the other three to those which took place in 2023.

The 24-year-old was remanded in custody following his arrest and appeared at Southern Derbyshire Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, where he was remanded to prison.



He is next due to appear at Derby Crown Court on September 10.

News.title: Homeless Brits starving on streets plead ‘look after us first!’ as small boat migrants ‘given priority treatment’
News.content:
HOMELESS Brits have told Andy Burnham “you need to look after your own first” as another wave of Channel migrants arrived in the UK.

The Sun spent three days speaking to dozens of rough sleepers across London’s streets, with many saying the Government has failed THEM while continuing to house asylum seekers in around 160 hotels across the UK.



While the Government provides accommodation to asylum seekers, homeless Brits have no automatic right to a roof over their heads.

It comes as Andy Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in the UK during his first speech as Prime Minister.



Bradley, 62, from London, became homeless after his marriage broke down and he moved into his mother’s council house.

But after she died just a few months later, he found out he was not entitled to live in the property so was evicted and left to sleep on the streets.



“Because I don’t have any addictions I’m not a priority. How does that make any sense? If I came over on a boat I’d be fine,” he said.

His comments come after a record 230 illegal immigrants crammed on to a single dinghy heading for Britain last week – landing taxpayers with an estimated £25million bill.

Once ashore, migrants are typically taken to the Home Office’s Manston processing centre before being moved into hotels, houses of multiple occupancy or former military sites while their asylum claims are considered.

Nearly 94,000 asylum seekers were living in government-funded accommodation at the end of March 2026, compared with the 4,793 people recorded by the Government as sleeping rough in England on a typical autumn night.

Former chef Paul, 59, who says he once cooked for the Queen Mother at Ardoe House in Aberdeen, lost his home after a relationship breakdown and a subsequent drug addiction.



After nearly 40 years of working in restaurants around the world, he is now begging for a sandwich outside Westminster Tube station.

Paul has been on and off the streets for the past four years. He claims to be now sober but claims there isn’t enough support for rough sleepers who aren’t substance users.

He said: “I’ve approached a few organisations here who say to me, because I’m not a drug addict or an alcoholic, that there’s nothing they can do for me because the system is set up just for those kinds of things.”



And without ID or a postal address, he says he can’t open a bank account to receive Universal Credit.

He claims a job centre worker told him to “rely on the kindness of strangers”.

Paul added that even if he had official documents and possessions, they would likely be stolen from him at night from other rough sleepers.

“Nobody has any honour anymore,” he said. “So what’s the point?”

When asked about the government-funded accommodation for asylum seekers, he responded: “Part of me thinks live and let live, and part of me thinks that 40 years ago this wouldn’t be happening.



“I think we’ve just diluted our whole identity down to something that now it’s normal for 60-year-old people to be sitting on the street, begging for food, having worked and lived here their whole lives.

“While people that have just arrived, [the Government is] quite happy to look after them and give them what they want. It’s hard not to be resentful. And apparently if you are resentful, that makes you a racist. So you can’t be resentful, apparently.”

He added: “And when it gets to the point that you’re probably better off in prison, because at least you’re getting three meals and a bed, that can’t be good either, can it?”



A parliamentary report found the Government spent £4.9billion on the asylum system in 2024-25, including £2.7billion on accommodation alone.

The Labour Government says they now have less than 160 hotels in use – down for 400 in 2023 – saving £1billion in accomodation costs since they took power and closing anohter 11 this week.

In comparison, the Government allocated £500million over a three-year period to help fund councils to reduce rough sleeping through outreach programmes and emergency accommodation in 2022.

On his first day as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping at the “earliest opportunity” and announced an additional £340million over the next five years.

But Tam, 62, from Glasgow, who has been sleeping rough for 40 years, said successive governments have failed to tackle the crisis.



Sitting outside a Leicester Square supermarket he claims: “Every government comes into Parliament trying to get rid of rough sleepers. It’s not going to happen.”

“If I was the Prime Minister, I would make sure to sort your own people first rather than treating all these people who are coming into the country.”

Tam said the Government had proved rough sleeping could be reduced during the pandemic, when emergency accommodation brought many people off the streets, but claimed many Brits had since ended up sleeping rough again.

Government figures suggest British nationals account for nearly two-thirds of all people sleeping rough.

While 13 per cent are from EU countries, 11 per cent are from non-EU countries and 11 per cent are unknown.



Kevin, 59, a Big Issue seller from London, became homeless after spending time in prison but is vague about his “petty” conviction.

He says his own family doesn’t know he’s living on the streets, but like many others who were interviewed, says his pride comes first.

Kevin believes more support should be targeted at Brits over asylum seekers who he says are given “special treatment”.



“I don’t mind anybody coming over for a different life if they’ve come from a war-torn area, but not just to come and think it’s about the NHS, come and sponge up the Government funding or come and just milk the system and get housing before our own people. They should be helping their own first before helping anyone else.”

Kevin believes homelessness services often fail people without addictions because they are housed alongside those with serious drink and drug problems, followed by little support to help them move into permanent accommodation.

He claimed: “It was a waste of my life. There was no proper move-on plan.”

Outside Charing Cross station, John from Galway, stands with a sleeping bag draped over his shoulders, wearing a pink cowboy hat he was given by a hen party.

He apparently served 16 years for armed burglary and says he has been on the streets for eight months.



John said he occasionally stays in a hostel but fights regularly break out in the night over drugs in the sweltering hostel room he shares with 20 other people.

“We should be looked after. People coming across in the boats, they’re getting hotels. They’re getting everything. We’re getting nothing. And we’re just being left, and that’s it.”

Former construction worker Paul, 44, from Oxford, says he has been sleeping rough for the past two years – also after leaving prison, where he spent four years serving a sentence for assault.

He says: “I shouldn’t be on the streets, there should be other people on the streets.

“They shouldn’t be letting people come over on boats and giving them houses and money every f***ing month when they can’t even help their own. I think that’s disgusting.”



Paul suffers from epilepsy and claims he has to beg for money to buy medication after he says authorities refused to prescribe the controlled drug he says he needs.

Migrants who are receiving Home Office asylum support are entitled to free NHS prescriptions, certain travel costs as well as housing.

According to the government website, asylum support is available to migrants if they are homeless or do not have money to buy food.



Asylum seekers can claim for housing and cash by filling out a 37-page government application if they are destitute or likely to become destitute within 14 days.

Migrants who have appealed their asylum decision or even had their application rejected can still apply for support while they arrange transport to return back to their country of origin.

Meanwhile, for homeless Brits, local authorities assess each applicant to determine what legal duty they are owed, with emergency accommodation generally reserved for those who are in a “priority need” category.

“Priority need” for accommodation includes pregnant women, households with children, victims of domestic abuse, vulnerable people or those made homeless by a disaster such as a flood or fire.

None of the rough sleepers who spoke to The Sun over a three-day period said they were categorised as a priority need.



Instead, they had all made their way to central London where they begged outside some of the biggest and busiest tourist attractions in the country.

London and the South East accounted for 43 per cent of all rough sleepers in autumn 2025, according to government data.

Westminster remains the local authority with the highest number of people sleeping rough with 360, followed by Camden (134), Somerset (103), the City of London (83), Bristol (70), Birmingham (68) and Leeds (65).

A Westminster City Council insider told The Sun it does more than any other local authority in the country to support people sleeping rough and invests £8million a year to help people come off the streets.

A spokesperson for the homeless charity St Mungo’s said: “Our Outreach teams are out on the streets day and night meeting thousands of people rough sleeping, all of whom have different life experiences and needs.



“These teams help people realise their needs, rights, and entitlements as the first step in moving away from the streets for good.

“We know however that we cannot tackle the moral tragedy of homelessness alone. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s announcement of ending rough sleeping on day one of his tenure is a galvanising moment for the sector, and for the people we support.

“We hope that this will bring greater coordination within government and improve access to statutory services. Only then can we close the cracks in support and ensure homelessness ends for good.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesperson said: “Ending rough sleeping is a personal commitment of the Prime Minister’s.

“He made the pledge on his first day in office and backed it immediately with an extra £340 million to tackle rough sleeping and homelessness across the country.”

News.title: Hugh Hefner ‘repeatedly warned FBI about Epstein’ after Playboy Playmate ‘was raped and trafficked by paedo financier’
News.content:
PLAYBOY founder Hugh Hefner repeatedly warned the FBI about Jeffrey Epstein after a model told him she was allegedly raped and trafficked by the paedophile financier, reports say.

Audra Lynn Christiansen made the claims to the late magazine publisher when she was 23 prompting him to alert authorities, according to a lawsuit.



The Playboy Playmate, who was Miss October 2003, reportedly told Hefner she was trafficked to a Macau casino billionaire named Stanley Ho, the filing says.

Ho, dubbed China’s “Godfather of gambling”, died in 2020.



Christiansen, now 46, asked Hefner to call the FBI on her behalf in 2005 as she believed the businessman had “clout” and connections in the agency.

Hefner reportedly called the FBI “multiple times”.

READ MORE US NEWS ESTATE HORROR Epstein's Zorro Ranch at centre of new lawsuit after claim of buried bodies

The complaint reads: “Mr. Hefner called the FBI multiple times on behalf of Ms. Christiansen to report Jeffrey Epstein.”

The revelations are part of an amended complaint filed in May in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida.



In the lawsuit, victims of Epstein claim FBI failed to act on multiple reports about his sexual abuse as early as 1996.

Jordan Merson, lawyer for the victims, told The New York Post: “The fact that the FBI is trying to utilize procedural technicalities to try to avert accountability and responsibility for its failures to properly investigate Jeffrey Epstein for over 20 years should be deeply concerning to all.

“How can you learn from errors if you do not acknowledge them?”



Christiansen, who once featured on the reality television series “The Girls Next Door”, was only contacted by the FBI in October 2020 following Epstein’s death.

The agency got in touch to follow up on the information provided 15 years ago, according to the lawsuit.

In her initial report, she claimed her agents introduced her to Epstein, who wanted to meet her after the release of a Playboy shoot where she featured.

Hefner himself was accused of rape five years after his 2017 death in the “Secrets of Playboy” documentary.

Several women in the film alleged he was a “predator” who was into bestiality.



The claims never made it to court and Hefner was never accused of rape while he was alive.

In the Epstein files released earlier this year by the Department of Justice, Ho is referred to as “the richest man in Hong Kong” in a 2011 email written by Epstein.

The disgraced financier tells a friend in the message Ho “owns most of Macau” and calls him “the leader of the Chinese mob”.

The FBI tried to get the lawsuit thrown out in June, saying it was “not required to investigate every complaint” it received.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The case is still ongoing in court.



Epstein died in 2019 in a New York jail cell while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

News.title: Ukraine blitzes Russian rocket & space plant with deadly Flamingo missiles in ‘huge blow to Putin’s Starlink system’
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin’s precious rocket and space centre in Russia – where the Kremlin is speculated to be developing its answer to Elon Musk’s Starlink – has been bombed.

Footage circulating on social media shows the TsSKB-Progress complex in the Samara region on fire and a column of smoke rising.



It is the key aerospace enterprise under Roscosmos, behind Soyuz-2 space rockets and Earth-observation satellites.

Ukrainian open-source group CyberBoroshno said the strike most likely hit Building 106A, where onboard equipment is installed on Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.



Analysts said: “Building 106A operates under a high cleanroom standard: this is where onboard electrical systems, instruments and printed circuit boards are installed – essentially the launch vehicle’s ‘nervous system’: the control system, cable network and instrumentation compartment.

“Without this stage, the rocket cannot be assembled, even when the body and tanks are ready.”



A major motive behind the attack may have been to disrupt the launches of Rassvet satellites – Russia’s answer to Starlink.

The Kremlin is racing to build its own low-orbit satellite Internet system to provide connections for its forces, and especially for long-range drones.



Ukraine gained an edge on the battlefield earlier this year after Musk was persuaded by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov to cut off access for Russia.

That majorly complicated communications and targeting in Putin’s war.

Now Russia is racing to build Rassvet, a copycat to SpaceX’s Starlink being developed by aerospace company Bureau 1440.

Ukraine is believed to have unleashed the domestically manufactured FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missile in the attack.

Volodymyr Zelensky boasted about the “new significant results” from the deep strike, which reached almost 600 miles inside Russia, measured from the Ukrainian border.



The Ukrainian President said: “In Samara region, one of the key enterprises within Roscosmos – the Progress Centre, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production – was hit.

“Flamingo missiles were used. A good achievement.”

News.title: Stop calling 999 to dob in your neighbours for having a barbecue, fire service begs after being swamped with calls
News.content:
FIRE services have begged Brits not to dob in their neighbours for having a barbecue after they were swamped with calls.

Millions of people across England and Wales received an emergency alert on their phones at around 7pm on Friday evening warning them of the risk of wildfires.



The government issued the alert warning people “not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks” with the country in the middle of another heatwave.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the request “came directly from Fire and Rescue Services”.



He urged Brits to take the alert “seriously” and “follow the guidance in place” as the UK contends with a series of devastating wildfires.

But the blaring alert sent panic across the nation, as fire services urged people not to call 999 to report their neighbours.

Surrey Fire and Rescue Service posted to X that they had received a “high volume of calls” urging people to call only if there “is an emergency or fire producing significant smoke”.

“We understand residents may be concerned, but we are unable to respond to reports of neighbours having BBQs, bonfires or campfires in their gardens unless there is an emergency,” they said.



“We support the Government’s message on this and would strongly advise against having bonfires, fireworks, campfires or disposable BBQs during this period.

“Fires can spread quickly and become difficult to control, putting your home and neighbouring properties at risk.”

Meanwhile, Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue said they were also experiencing “exceptionally high call volumes”.

They added that they understood the public’s “vigilance” but said to only call 999 if there is a “genuine emergency or immediate risk to life, property or the environment”.

The message was also echoed by South Wales Fire and Rescue Service who urged the public to only call for ” a new emergency”.



It comes after nineteen homes were destroyed after a wildfire grew out of control in Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday.

The blaze left “extensive damage” and resulted in dozens of people needing to be treated by paramedics and evacuated from their homes.

Other locations in the UK have also been affected by wildfires in recent days.

There were multiple reported across the Midlands yesterday, including also in Stoke-on-Trent, Birmingham, Warwickshire and Worcestershire – as well as others in Norfolk and Wales.

Chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) Phil Garrigan told BBC Breakfast that fire services have been called to 43 new wildfires in the last 24 hours with 11 major incidents declared in the last two days.



He added that nine firefighters have been taken to hospital in the last 48 hours for smoke inhalation after “taking courageous actions”.

The surge in fires came as the UK officially broke its 2026 record for the hottest day on Thursday, with the mercury hitting 38.5C in Kew Gardens, London.

Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, said the UK’s Emergency Alert system “reflects the seriousness with which the government is acting to safeguard people and property”.

“During this period of extreme heat, we are asking people to take simple steps to limit the risk of further fires,” she continued.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The government will continue to provide every assistance to communities being impacted by these fires, including the deployment of 100 additional military personnel in major incident areas.”



But the deafening siren sparked a furious backlash with some questioning whether the ear-splitting warning was necessary.

News.title: Glam fitness influencer, 28, among seven killed in horror head on smash in high speed police chase
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FATAL CHASE Glam fitness influencer, 28, among seven killed in horror head on smash in high speed police chase

AN INFLUENCER has been killed alongside six other people in a head-on crash while fleeing police.

Alana Alves da Silva, 28, was allegedly hauling 137kg of cannabis when the Fiat Cronos she was travelling in smashed into an oncoming car.



Better known online as Vampira 085, the content creator was pronounced dead at the scene in Minas Gerais State, Brazil.

The incident unfolded on the BR-251 highway on Saturday last week.



Police had attempted to stop the vehicle near the town of Salinas but the driver allegedly ignored their order and sped away.

A high-speed pursuit then continued for six miles before the Fiat swerved into oncoming traffic while overtaking on a bend and then crashed into a Chevrolet Astra.

Alana was one of four people in the Fiat. Two young men who were also travelling with her died in hospital.

A woman, 20, survived but remains in a critical condition with severe head injuries and multiple fractures.

All four men travelling in the Chevrolet, aged between 46 and 79, were killed in the disaster.

Police identified the suspected driver of the Fiat as Pedro Yan Linhares Gutierrez, 24.



Officers said he did not have a driving licence, was wearing an electronic tag and was already facing drug trafficking charges.

In the aftermath, the highway was completely shut off.

Alana had built a large online fanbase – boasting over 59,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok – by sharing daily workout tips and healthy living content and comedy skits.



She also ran her own online fitness fashion shop from her home in the city of Fortaleza.

The investigation into the fatal crash remains ongoing.

News.title: Our chocolate-box village was made famous by Downton Abbey – now plans for 200 new homes could destroy our countryside
News.content:
FEELING DOWN Our chocolate-box village was made famous by Downton Abbey – now plans for 200 new homes could destroy our countryside

LOCALS are outraged that their scenic village, once the backdrop to a beloved British TV series, could be swamped with 200 newbuilds.

The quaint community of Bampton, Oxfordshire, was once the location for the fictional Yorkshire village in Downton Abbey.



ITV began filming on the cobbled streets of the picturesque village in 2010, with Bampton becoming a global tourist attraction almost overnight.

Several scenes in the series, including the Old Rectory and parish church, were filmed in the village – with the iconic Highclere Castle located just 40 miles away.



Residents now fear plans for 200 new homes could risk overdeveloping the site, with several complaints lodged with the West Oxfordshire District Council.

Dr William Outhwaite wrote: “Bampton has already been massively damaged by excessive and insensitive building programmes which have overloaded its medical, educational and other infrastructure.



“This proposal would add the loss of agricultural land and of a still attractive site on the edge of the village.”

Hourigan Planning submitted a blueprint for 190 homes, 40 per cent of which they claim would be affordable housing.

But many locals fear the added strain on resources and existing infrastructure could cause flooding, as seen back in 2007.

One said: “We moved here 28 years ago because we wanted to live in a village – it’s a shame how places like Bampton become overdeveloped with no real infrastructure to cope with such influx of houses.



”Very sad that countryside is being lost at such a colossal rate affecting wildlife and country life.”

Another asked: “Do we really need more homes?

“My water pressure is already poor and no need to mention doctors appointments.”

Locals have previously spoken out about the perils of living in a tourist hotspot – despite the handsome cash flow – with many objecting to the “brash American accents” on their doorsteps.



Bus loads of American fans, intrigued by the historical drama’s depiction of early 20th-century Britain, come armed with cameras and selfie sticks to Bampton.

“My friend overheard a tour guide say that Bampton was nothing before Downton Abbey,” said village local Fabrizio Manerba, 62.

”Let me tell you – Bampton was a beautiful, expensive place to live long beforehand.”

Just last year, the village was named as one of the most beautiful chocolate box villages in England, according to Independent Cottages.

Qualifying factors include the number of historic buildings, the oldest recorded existence of the village and whether it’s classed as an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.



Fabrizio, who lives in the main square, complains that the tourists often stand in his driveway and “just go everywhere”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Around 10 buses a day were seen during the town’s peak popularity, according to locals, with visitors lingering and posing for photographs.

A spokesperson for Hourigan Planning said: “The scheme would comprise a mix of both open market homes and affordable homes, and includes significant areas of accessible open space.”

News.title: Brutal storm strikes Brit holiday hotspot as torrential rain & hailstones wreak havoc with flood alert triggered
News.content:
A BRUTAL storm has struck the Costa del Sol with torrential rain and hailstones sparking a flood alert in the Brit holiday hotspot.

Urgent weather warnings have been issued across Spain‘s southern coast as thunderstorms wreak havoc during the peak summer getaway season.



Shocked holidaymakers arriving at Malaga Airport in the early hours of this morning were met with biblical rain and powerful gusts of wind.

Jaw-dropping footage showed scores of panicked Brit tourists waiting out the dramatic downpour.



Hailstones were also seen striking the airport tarmac while lightning bolts were filmed tearing through the night sky.

The heavy deluge battered the Costa del Sol and Malaga City – with tourists currently flocking to the region for summer trips.



The harsh weather – which could trigger flash flooding – is expected to continue throughout this weekend.

Large swathes of the Andalusia region are expected to see drastic changes in weather with storms, flooding, and large hailstones, local authorities say.



Spanish weather agency Aemet has predicted a so-called Dana system to sweep through the region.

It is essentially a cold drop isolated depression – meaning huge amounts of rain can fall in just hours.

Up to 20mm of rain could fall in just one hour, according to Aemet.



The yellow warnings for thunderstorms will be in place from 2pm to 10pm today.

On Friday, Almería, Granada and Jaén issued storm warnings.

But the region will see stark contrasts between showers and sun as record-breaking levels of heat also continue to persist.



Amber alerts for the heatwave remained in place in Córdoba and Jaén, where temperatures could reach 40C.

Cádiz, Granada, Huelva and Seville are also set to remain on yellow alert.

Over the weekend, showers and thunderstorms are expected to batter the Costa del Sol as well as the Balearic Islands of Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca.

Hailstones are expected to develop during the weather phenomenon.

From Monday onwards, the risk of widespread storms is set to decrease.



Over the weekend, today is estimated to be the most challenging day of the shocking turn of weather.

The heaviest showers will hit the north of Catalonia and Aragón, according to local media.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Throughout the day, rain is expected to hit many eastern regions, including Valencia, Murcia and eastern Andalusia.

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham has described the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday as "a tragedy on so many levels," as he called for a "moment for reflection".

Arday was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgement. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," he told broadcasters during a visit to Cornwall.

In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They said a "campaign of misinformation" had been too much for him.

Arday, 41, resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

A friend told the BBC Arday had described feeling "destroyed" and had told him his travel visa to the US had been revoked.

Eamonn McCrystal, who became his friend at St Mary's University College London, tried to reassure him what he was going through would pass, but Arday replied "it does not feel like it will."

Eamonn told the BBC "He was the nicest person. So kind and such a gentle soul.

"We shared an office at university, when I set up the student radio station, and he used to speak on the station a lot"

"I'm in shock, I can't believe it."

The University of Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice led the tributes, saying the faculty was "desperately saddened" to learn of his death.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" to hear about the death and she urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan is among those who have said Arday was subjected to unrelenting media scrutiny.

He said Arday had faced "an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse", adding that he was a victim of "a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced".

"His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us," he posted on X.

Jo Grady, General secretary of the University and College Union said the "level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to has been sickening" and "must be investigated".

Lord Paul Boateng, who became the UK's first black cabinet minister in 2002 when he was appointed Chief Secretary to the Treasury under Tony Blair, told BBC Newsnight he was " horrified, shocked and deeply saddened".

"Racism in academia is a fact of life and needs to be addressed," he added in a written statement.

In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to "a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism".

"The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target," he said.

Director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge, Prof Simon Baron-Cohen told the Today programme Arday had been "bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud".

"He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man," he said.

He spoke to Arday the morning of his death, and said the academic had felt unable to leave the house.

"He has experienced what he described as a campaign against him, for the last three years," he previously told BBC News.

"What he was saying to me was 'they've destroyed my life' - it's not clear who they were but I think he was referring to the media."

"The personal attacks on him have been so immense.

"This isn't to point fingers, and its not a single media outlet, but in the last few weeks since he resigned, I must have received a hundred new requests - to comment on his life."

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
Jason Arday had beaten what would have been an impressive international field of candidates to a top job in a university ranked in the global top 10.

However, in July 2026 questions about the quality of his academic research, which some had raised privately with him, broke into the open.

These included an allegation that parts of his first major piece of research, a PhD awarded by Liverpool John Moores University, were plagiarised. In other words it was suggested he had used the work of another academic without adequately crediting them.

Arday said this was untrue and Liverpool John Moores University said after a review that it stood by the quality of the research. Arday suggested any mistakes in attribution were due to his autism.

Newspapers dissected Arday's previous work while at Durham and Glasgow universities, and on social media, academics were divided between those publicly championing the black autistic academic and those who said his work did not withstand analysis.

Rows about research rarely break through into national debate but this was Cambridge, an elite university whose history and reputation has been built on excellence in research, original thinking and academic integrity.

For many academics, including many at Cambridge, robust scrutiny of the integrity of research is a red line. Some wrote to the vice chancellor demanding an independent inquiry because they felt the reputation of the university was at stake.

There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Jason Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Jason Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family. He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Jason Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Jason Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Jason Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Jason Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Jason Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Jason Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, General Secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: Heathrow Airport pipe leak causes flood disruption
News.content:
Heathrow Airport has warned access to Terminals 2 and 3 is restricted because of flooding caused by a leak in a pipe within the grounds of the airport.

Water in the central terminal area means anyone trying to travel to or from either of these terminals cannot travel by road. Instead passengers are being advised to travel by rail and Tube and to avoid using cars.

An airport spokesperson said: "Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible, we apologise for any disruption caused," adding: "The leak has been isolated and repairs are on-going."

The disruption comes during the school holidays, one of the busiest periods for the airport.

Heathrow said 19 July was its busiest day of the year so far as many schools broke up for summer, with 267,000 passengers passing through.

The airport was recently affected by disruption to railway services, after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel.

News.title: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?
News.content:
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering.

"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope."

Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change?

The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response.

Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working.

News.title: Europe's scorched landscapes seen from space after summer heatwaves
News.content:
The impact of this summer's extreme temperatures on western Europe can now be seen from space after successive heatwaves since May.

Satellite images examined by BBC Verify show shrunken glaciers, scorched areas left by wildfires, green fields turned arid and lower river levels.

And some landmarks have been affected, too. The Palace of Versailles, south of the French capital Paris, appears as an island of trees surrounded by brown fields in these images.

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: I wish I had been a more rebellious teenager, says Bella Ramsey
News.content:
Bella Ramsey spent many teenage years working with adults so never really went through the moody, rebellious phase often associated with being a teenager.

The British actor, who debuted in Game of Thrones aged 11 and uses they/them pronouns, says they had consciously decided not to behave like a stereotypical teenager after hearing criticisms from adults.

"I was like, I'm not going to be that."

So when Sunny Dancer, a film about a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, gave Ramsey seven weeks to experience teenage freedom, it was an opportunity to dive straight in.

"I got to be a teenager aged 21, which was brilliant," Ramsey tells BBC News. "It was really nice - and liberating."

Looking back, Ramsey says the experience made them wonder whether they had missed out by being quite so sensible the first time around.

"I kind of wish that I had made the most of being a teenager and getting away with things and being a bit rebellious."

In Sunny Dancer, Ramsey plays Ivy, a young female cancer survivor in remission who reluctantly heads to a "chemo camp" where she finds an unexpected group of friends and has a summer that changes her.

News.title: Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed
News.content:
Fires across England and Wales have prompted a national government alert warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The warning on Friday evening came as it was revealed 19 homes were destroyed and a further 18 damaged in a huge fire in Stourbridge, West Midlands, that spread rapidly through grass and woodland on Thursday before damaging homes.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told members of the public to take the warning "seriously", adding it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents the service had ever dealt with.

It was one of several fires being dealt with across England and Wales on Friday.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed

Overnight in to Saturday, four 14-year-olds from Porth, South Wales, have all been arrested on suspicion of arson and have since been bailed under investigation

In Hampshire, firefighters spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, Hampshire, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath, off Gurney Road in the city.

Elsewhere in the West Midlands fires caused extensive damage in Warstock and Kings Norton, Birmingham on Thursday. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life .

In Stoke-on-Trent on Thursday four homes in Sandyford were destroyed, with other properties damaged. Two people were arrested on suspicion of arson. Six firefighters were taken to hospital due to smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

In Willenhall, West Midlands, at least three homes and several gardens were destroyed in fires on Stonehouse Avenue and Harry Perks Street.

Investigators said they were working with other emergency services to establish how the Stourbridge fire started, with police saying they were keeping an open mind.

Some of the worst-affected areas have been cordoned off and many residents who were evacuated, including the Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverend Martin Gorick, have not been able to return home.

News.title: Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
News.content:
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.

After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.

Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.

The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.

News.title: New Forest fire fully contained, fire service says
News.content:
A wildfire that broke out in the New Forest on Sunday is now "fully surrounded", says the fire service.

The blaze began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday, with 23 drivers having to abandon their vehicles as the fire took hold.

The A31 will remain closed until at least Thursday 20 August, says National Highways.

In an update on Saturday, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said: "Overnight, firefighters continued working incredibly hard at the scene, and the fire is now fully surrounded. We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The fire service revealed on Friday evening that the blaze has affected an area of approximately 1.6 sq km (0.6 sq miles) and 169 fire appliances have attended from 93 fire stations.

In the update on Friday, assistant chief fire officer for HIWFRS Rob Cole said: "I'm pleased to say we are getting on top of this. However there are many days of work ahead of us to ensure that this fire doesn't spread when the wind blows or when other hotspots start to occur."

On Friday evening the UK's mobile phone alert system was used to warn people not to light anything which could spark a wildfire, including barbecues and garden incinerators.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told members of the public to take the warning "seriously" and said it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

News.title: Six people arrested after man abducted in Edinburgh
News.content:
Six people have been arrested in East Lothian after a man was abducted in Edinburgh.

Police Scotland said it received a report that a man had been abducted in the Canonmills area of the capital at about 22:30 on Thursday.

A 22-year-old man was later traced in Longniddry on Friday and taken to hospital as a precaution.

Five men - aged 21, 21, 22, 23 and 45 - and a 40-year-old woman have been arrested and police say inquiries are ongoing.

A section of the A198, which runs through the village of Longniddry, has been shut by police and a diversion is in place.

Officers believe this was a targeted incident and there is no risk to the wider public.

Det Insp Robbie Wallace said: "We understand an incident of this nature will be concerning but please be assured our inquiries are ongoing.

"Police will remain in the Longniddry area while this investigation continues and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers."

One report on social media said armed officers had been seen removing someone from a car.

Lothian Buses posted that some services were unable to serve the village and its routes had been diverted due to the road closure.

Longniddry is a coastal village about 15 miles (24km) from Canonmills.

News.title: Derailed Essex train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Two dead after light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two people have died following a light aircraft crash in north Wales.

The aircraft was found in a remote location close to Trawsfynydd, Gwynedd, with the two people on board pronounced dead at the scene, North Wales Police said.

The force received reports shortly after 12:00 BST that a light aircraft travelling from an airfield in England had not arrived at Caernarfon Airport as scheduled.

Multi-agency air and ground searches were carried out until the aircraft was found.

A spokesperson for the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said: "An investigation has been launched and a multidisciplinary team of inspectors are on their way to the accident site."

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal ‘lead race’ to sign £50m target, Tottenham reach Gakpo ‘agreement’, Fernandez latest
News.content:
Arsenal could turn their attention to Brighton’s £51m-rated midfielder Jack Hinshelwood as they continue talks with Bayer Leverkusen over signing England international Jarell Quansah. The Premier League champions have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and the 23-year-old Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.

Meanwhile, Barcelona are set to make a third bid of around £60m for Rodri, but are still set to fall £10m short of Manchester City’s valuation of the Ballon d’Or winner. The deal could yet influence the speed of any move for Enzo Fernandez, with his former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca pushing for the midfielder's signature. Chelsea’s deadline of 5pm on Friday passed without City submitting their £120m bid, and the club expect Fernandez to now stay for the upcoming season.

Tottenham have agreed personal terms with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, according to reports in the Netherlands, while Spurs are also close to signing Manchester City winger Savinho and have joined Manchester United and Arsenal in expressing interest in Galatasaray forward Victor Osimhen. Arsenal’s Gabriel Martinelli has rejected the chance to join the Turkish club as part of a deal.

In other news, Tottenham captain Cristian Romero has completed his transfer to Atletico Madrid, while Paris Saint-Germain have confirmed the signing of Ferran Torres, the scorer of the winning goal in the World Cup final, from Barcelona. Crystal Palace have completed the signing of right-sided player Anan Khalaili on a five-year contract.

News.title: Burnham warned not to dash hopes for indefinite prisoners: ‘Do not sell them another dream’
News.content:

The prime minister has been urged not to dash the hopes of thousands of prisoners trapped on indefinite jail terms after he pledged to find a resolution to the “long-running injustice”.

Andy Burnham is facing calls to revisit proposals to appoint a specialist panel of former and serving high court judges to review the cases of almost 2,300 prisoners serving controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences.

It comes after he vowed to address the legacy of the “clearly unfair” open-ended jail terms as part of potential measures to ease prison overcrowding and curb early release plans. His comments this week were a major breakthrough for IPP prisoners languishing without a release date, an issue The Independent has campaigned to end.

Labour MP Kim Johnson, who has long called for IPP reform, has urged the prime minister and justice secretary Alex Norris not to dash their hopes as he prepares a plan to present to Parliament in September.

Writing exclusively in The Independent, she said: “For those who have spent years trapped in the abolished sentence, and for the families who have suffered alongside them, a glimmer of hope can be incredibly powerful.

“But if that hope is once again raised only to be snatched away, it will deepen an already profound injustice. These prisoners do not need another promise of a review. They need justice.”

open image in gallery Labour MP Kim Johnson ( AFP/Getty )

The Liverpool Riverside MP said the jail terms, which were abolished in 2012 but not retroactively, remain one of the greatest stains on our criminal justice system.

The government is facing legal action after the United Nations, which has long raised concerns the punishment causes psychological torture, found some IPP prisoners are being arbitrarily detained in a damning legal opinion issued last month.

“The UN has described their continued impact as perpetuating serious human rights violations, with UN experts warning that the prolonged uncertainty under the IPP regime is causing serious psychological deterioration, including self-harm and an increased risk of suicide,” Ms Johnson added. “That is the reality of this dreadful sentence.

“More than a decade after IPPs were abolished, we still have people trapped in an indeterminate sentence that parliament itself has rejected. Behind every IPP prisoner is a person who has been through the same agonising cycle over and over again: parole hearings, preparation for release, hope that this might finally be the moment they can come home – followed by another refusal and another indefinite period behind bars.

“We cannot allow for this to happen ever again.

“If the justice secretary’s review produces another report, another set of recommendations and another promise to look at the issue in the future, that would be more than inadequate. After all these years, it would honestly be cruel.”

open image in gallery Burnham has urged his justice secretary, Alex Norris to review IPP terms ( Getty )

She called for a resentencing or reconsideration exercise, suggesting proposals raised at the start of the year for a judge-led reconsideration panel to be “brought back and developed”.

The idea was previously raised in an unsuccessful amendment to the Sentencing Act brought by former Conservative solicitor general Lord Edward Garnier, who has also urged the prime minister to look again at the idea.

It was backed by the UN special rapporteur on torture, Dr Alice Jill Edwards, who said in January it was a “pragmatic compromise that could pave the way toward individualised and just outcomes for those affected”, adding: “Something must be done to prevent the continuation of what has become a never-ending saga of injustice and cruelty.”

Under the proposals, a panel of 12 serving and former judges would review each case – considering the prisoner’s offending, how long they have served, their risk to the public and what support they would need in the community – and decide whether they should be released on licence. However, if the justice secretary disagrees with the panel’s decision to free a prisoner, they would have the power to decline their release.

In cases where the prisoner is suffering from a mental disorder or would present a risk to the public or themselves on release, judges would also consider whether they should be transferred to hospital for treatment.

open image in gallery UN special rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards previously backed the idea of a judicial reconsideration exercise ( AFP/Getty )

Ms Johnson said: “Putting the process back in the hands of the judiciary would provide the legal safeguards and independence that this issue requires. Those who no longer pose a risk should be able to have their sentence reconsidered and, where appropriate, released under properly resourced supervision in the community.”

She continued: “I’ll be pushing for the prime minister not to give IPP prisoners another glimmer of hope to then snatch it away.

“Hear their cases, reconsider their sentences and properly resource the support they need when coming back to their communities.

“After years of injustice, they need a fair and workable pathway to freedom. It is time to end this grave miscarriage of justice once and for all.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "It is right that these sentences were abolished, and as the IPP annual report shows, support has significantly improved for these offenders, with greater access to rehabilitation and mental health support. We are now looking at what more can be done.

“As we have set out, the justice secretary is reviewing reforms to these unjust sentences."

News.title: Holly Willoughby ‘mortified’ after wardrobe malfunction on children’s TV ‘landed her on Page 3’
News.content:
Holly Willoughby said she was “mortified” after a wardrobe malfunction on a children’s TV show “landed her on Page 3”.

In the latest episode of Holly Willoughby Together, the 45-year-old was joined by Spice Girls’ Emma Bunton and All Saints’ Nicole Appleton, where they discussed fashion mishaps.

Willoughby explained that whilst presenting an episode of ITV’s Ministry of Mayhem in 2004, her top broke whilst she was dancing for a segment involving boyband Blue, leaving her “left boob swinging”.

After the show went for an advert break, she asked producers if they had seen the wardrobe malfunction. “We’re not going to lie to you. We did see it,” they told her.

“And then The Sun put me on Page 3 the next day. So I’ve been a Page 3 girl with my boob out,” she claimed.

Bluey and her sister Bingo are featured running away as a balloon pops in the first-look trailer for The Bluey Movie.

The big-screen adaptation of the popular Australian animated children’s television series, centred around a family of heeler dogs, will arrive in cinemas on August 6, 2027.

In the first trailer for the film, Bluey can be heard shouting “good one, Bingo”, as the balloon is punched into the air, to which Bingo replies “thanks, Bluey”.

As the balloon drops back down, the pair scream as they accidentally push the balloon forwards rather than upwards, and Bluey shouts “don’t let it touch the ground”.

The siblings then race after the balloon, but it lands on the grass and the pair run away before it pops to reveal the film’s title.

Premiered at Disney’s D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event, the film’s producers said it “takes place on an action-packed day when a big surprise changes everything for Bluey and her family”.

At the fan event, there was a surprise game of keepy-uppy with the balloons from the trailer for fans, while a poster for the film, featuring Bluey and a balloon, was also released.

The movie will be written and directed by Bluey creator Joe Brumm and produced by Ludo Studio, which makes the show, in collaboration with BBC Studios.

The show follows the exhaustible and imaginative blue heeler, Bluey, and Bingo, along with their mother Chilli and father Bandit.

The film will feature voice talent from the series, including Melanie Zanetti as Chilli and David McCormack as Bandit.

While most episodes are about seven minutes long, creator Brumm experimented with a longer episode to end the third series in 2024.

Available in more than 140 countries, Bluey is the number one show for children on CBeebies and Disney+ in the UK.

Disney will release the Bluey movie in cinemas worldwide, followed by streaming on Disney+.

Last Month, the show’s award-winning producer Sam Moor said “it felt like a natural step” for the show to be translated into an Australian Indigenous language for the first time, and the team is “very keen” to do more.

The children’s series recently translated five of its episodes from seasons one and two into Yolnu Matha, the Australian First Nations language of north-east Arnhem Land.

A quick-thinking air traffic controller averted a potential disaster on Friday after noticing two American Airlines jets were mistakenly flying the same flight number.

Audio of the incident shortly after midnight Friday shows how the Phoenix controller found a solution to ensure the planes that were both called American 2482 maintained proper separation as one plane arrived from Chicago shortly after the other had taken off.

“I’ve been working air traffic for 25 years. I’ve never seen two aircraft pretty much merge with the same call sign. That’s pretty incredible,” the controller said after the departing plane had safely cleared the area.

If both pilots thought the controller was telling them to fly at the same altitude as they headed toward each other, they might have collided.

Therefore, it was crucial that the two pilots knew which plane he was directing.

The audio posted by ATC.com shows how the controller quickly started referring to “American 2482 on the arrival” and “American 2482 on the departure” to keep the two planes straight.

The controller kept the arriving plane safely above the departing plane even as their flight paths converged and made sure that the pilots of both airlines saw each other when they were still miles apart. He also directed the departing plane not to climb too high, so a gap would remain between the planes.

“It could have been disastrous, but I’m glad it worked out,” the controller said afterwards.
