World.title: Residents need waste education, not more bin nights
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Residents need waste education, not more bin nights August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Waste education key

The state Liberals propose weekly rubbish bin collection. But what about when we run out of landfill sites? Instead of encouraging more rubbish, why not educate people on how to reduce waste? This would be a longer-term and more environmental solution.

Our family was inspired by a couple who went a year without putting their landfill bin out. We composted all our food scraps, tissues and paper towels in a worm farm and composting bays, which Imade from pallets . I covered them up with chook-wire to keep the rats and possums out. (Dog poo’s OK too, as long as you don’t put it on your veggies.) We bought a set of washable nappies, refilled containers with shampoo, laundry powder and honey from the local wholefoods store. And tried to buy products that had minimal or recyclable packaging. All the soft plastics, we bagged and took to Woolies.

After six months of not putting our bin out, a tatty old pillow tipped us over the edge. That was a couple of years ago. But now, thanks to Liberals leader Jess Wilson, we’re fired up to see if we can beat our PB.

Grant Morgan, Hurstbridge Priorities amiss

Angus Taylor, Andrew Bragg and Tim Wilson have done no favours to ordinary Australians with their plans to gut the National Construction Code. Wilson says lower income earners should just “put on a jumper” in colder weather. They propose reducing regulation including energy efficiency. Wow. They (say they) will make housing cheaper and make owners (and renters) pay for it with increased energy use for the life of the building. They decry the cost of energy on the one hand but on the other hand they will make us all use more of it. If people should just get used to the weather, they could start by turning off the heating and cooling in Parliament House.

Chris Curnow, Skye Outrageous spending

For the Bayside Council to propose spending $40,000 to forensically research how the endangered Growling Grass Frogs first arrived at the site of the Yalukit William Nature Reserve, in Brighton, is outrageous (″⁣How did frogs get to Brighton? For council, it’s a $40,000 question″⁣, 13/8). Our rates should be spent on protecting and preserving endangered species, including frogs, not a witch-hunt. The volunteers for the Yalukit William Nature Reserve Association, who care for this site, should be applauded and encouraged by the council, for their work.

Caroline Shepard, Brighton



Look to the birds

Growling Grass Frogs used to be common in the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, although their presence has no doubt been affected by the recent worldwide decline in frog populations due to a fungal disease

While it is comforting to learn that this frog species is once again thriving in a Brighton nature reserve, it is also laughable to learn that Bayside Council is considering spending $40,000 to dispel a claim that they were illegally transported from Melbourne’s west. If indeed the species has only recently arrived at the reserve it is more likely that the frog eggs were transported there by water birds, which is a common method of distribution.

John Lambrick, Malvern Heat problems

They are shutting down nuclear sites in Europe because of the heatwaves causing lack of water. What say those who want them here in our climate?

Ross Hosking, Blackwood, SA Power of policies

Sussan Ley says her bus trip through America was to try to find ″⁣clarity″⁣. She has talked about people whose lives were in transition and disarray, and people who are disconnected from politics and the ways of government, and those whose lives are characterised by a lifetime of being overlooked.

It is somewhat disingenuous to speak of people as being ″⁣overlooked″⁣ without acknowledging the structural conditions that leave people overlooked in the first place. Chronic, grinding poverty, insecure housing, inadequate access to health and social services, and persistent economic exclusion are not incidental to people’s disconnection from government.

These are not simply personal circumstances. Disconnection is shaped by policy choices, the distribution of resources and access to opportunity. If we are serious about understanding people who feel overlooked, we need to look beyond their disconnection and examine the structural conditions that produce it. Clarify is what governments must do: to make the connections between people’s lived experiences and the policies that shape them and allocating resources to address disadvantage rather than simply describing its consequences. Every government has a responsibility to improve the lives of its citizens, particularly those who do not have the income and resources necessary to live a decent and secure life.

Dr Helen Keleher, Professor (Adj) Monash University The correct usage

Not to sound pedantic, but Nikki Barrowclough’s piece (“About time we got our heads around correct grammar”, 14/08) wasn’t about grammar at all. It was about usage. She has noticed the relentless rise in the popularity of around in place of alternative prepositions such as concerning or regarding. She has put her finger on a trend that she finds annoying, and many of us would agree with her. But none of her examples seem to be ungrammatical; they are just questions of usage or style.

By contrast, it would be very bad grammar to say “I’m sick of him hanging around I”, instead of “around me”. In English, prepositions are followed by nouns or pronouns in the objective or accusative case, like him or me.

Justin McDermott, West Brunswick Sides of a coin

Your correspondent (Letters, 15/8) argues that private school funding alleviates strain on state schools, but how do we justify a system where 98 per cent of our private schools are funded above the School Resourcing Standard and 98 per cent of public schools below this standard?

Productivity Commission data shows that over the 2023-24 period non-government school spending per student grew 27.5 per cent versus 5 per cent for government schools. A UNICEF report has described the Australian education system as one of the most unequal in the developed world.

In the end, it is not about who pays for what, but about the sort ofsociety we want, and we are accepting a divided educational system that would not be tolerated by any other visionary country.

Bryan Long, Balwyn



A hipster the PM is not

Can we just move on from the PM’s stupid remark about melons? He was trying to be hip and failed miserably. Surely there must be more important things on the agenda.

Ian Anderson, Ascot Vale Fruits of sadness

Ditch the influencers prime minister, we would rather not know their opinion – it only leads to melancholia.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading Spoils of war

So now we need to buy a missile system to protect the AUKUS submarines we may never see. MAGA has become MARA – Make Americans Richer Again.

Pete Garfield, Echuca Bin, and gone

Following his defeat in the Clacton byelection in the UK, I guess the Count is now, sadly, a bit of a has-bin.

Paul Sands, Sunbury The real thing

The country sends all its loving to you, Johnny. Young Talent Time was such good fun. Smiley is a great anti-war song. You were the real thing. Tomorrow, we’ll miss you.

Ann Rennie, Surrey Hills

World.title: Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAnimals Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets Neil Vigdor August 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was not a moment to spare. The doors to the TriMet bus, which was heading west on Tuesday morning towards downtown Portland, Oregon, had started to close when they opened for two stragglers. Loading Neither paid the fare. Kids ride free – or so they thought.



Not in the case of these two juvenile goats, which transit officials and police said had escaped from their enclosure and ventured onto a lime green FX2-Division bus. Security camera footage chronicled their strange escapade, showing some other passengers doing a double take before shooing the goats off the bus after the driver reopened the doors. Their jaunt prompted 911 calls and drew comparisons in Portland to the famous 2002 foray of a coyote that wandered onto a light rail MAX train, which was not in service at the time, and inspired a music video and another song. “They don’t have a valid pass,” the driver playfully told the other passengers as the goats exited the bus. The goats belong to a family that lives less than two blocks from the bus stop and are named Billy the Kid and Billy the Goat, Lrae Anderson, who identified himself as the owner, said on Friday.



“I couldn’t believe that they actually went across the busy street and tried to get on the bus and all that,” Anderson said. “They got on like they’ve done it before.” Related Article MIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Anderson, 48, a rapper who also goes by the name Copper Loc, said his children — he has four sons — sometimes forgot to close the gate of the goats’ enclosure. A neighbour brought the goats back to their home the same day, Anderson said, noting that he had since installed a lock and improved the fencing.



Anderson said the family had acquired the goats about three months ago after moving to the property at the suggestion of a friend, who told him they would feed on plentiful blackberries from sticker bushes on the property. Since their escape he had learnt that they were pygmy goats, he said. Footage of the horned interlopers, which TriMet posted last week to Instagram, had amassed more than 5.4 million views, according to the transit agency. “The video of them boarding the bus has definitely sparked something in people’s imaginations,” Tyler Graf, a spokesperson for TriMet, said in an email on Friday. But not every passenger paid much attention to the escapees, video footage from inside the bus showed.



“I see the one lady,” Anderson said. “She’s sitting there, and she’s on her phone and she didn’t even notice the goats on the bus. I was like, ‘What are they doing?’” Two loose pygmy goats unexpectedly wandered onto a bus in Portland, Oregon. TRIMET As he was preparing for a hip-hop show in Seattle scheduled for Saturday, Anderson said the episode had provided musical inspiration. “I’ve already started making a song about the goats,” he said. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Live: NZ Warriors v Brisbane Broncos at Suncorp Stadium
World.content:
NZ Warriors take on reigning NRL champions Brisbane Broncos for the second time this season at Suncorp Stadium, with a top-two spot on the competition table up for grabs.

A commanding win could see them edge ahead of Penrith Panthers in the standings, but they must overcome a wounded Broncos outfit lying in the long grass, waiting to spring an ambush.

World.title: Canterbury hold out Bay of Plenty to retain Ranfurly Shield
World.content:
Canterbury have held on to the Ranfurly Shield with a thrilling 33-28 win over Bay of Plenty at Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch.

It was their first defence - after they beat Otago last weekend - but it was looking decidedly shaky with 14 minutes to go when the scores were locked at 28-all.

It had been 21-7 to Canterbury at halftime, with the holders notching three tries after having a decided edge in possession and territory.

Bay of Plenty scored just before halftime from a tap penalty, but their challenge looked to be going backwards when Ngane Punivai scored for Canterbury early in the second half.

But the momentum shifted big-time with the Steamers roaring back into the game, scoring three tries to level up the scores.

Canterbury hit back with a try to Toby Bell with 10 minutes to go and then had some nervous moments after a try by Andrew Knewstubb was ruled out. Bay of Plenty mounted a sustained attack taking the game into added time before a knock-on sealed their fate.

Canterbury will defend the shield again on Thursday when they host Northland.

In other matches on Saturday, Otago scored three tries in the last 10 minutes to pip Manawatū 29-27 in Palmerston North, while Hawke's Bay came from behind to beat Auckland 44-31.

World.title: Water main bursts in Porirua, causing hours of disruption
World.content:
A burst water main in Porirua was being repaired on Saturday night, with water outages expected to end around 10.30pm.

A 300mm main burst on Mepham Place around 2:20pm on Saturday, causing asphalt on the road to crack.

That led to outages for the city centre, Rānui, and Elsdon.

"It is anticipated that service will be interrupted for at least eight hours," mayor Anita Baker said on Saturday afternoon.

Pātaka Art + Museum, Café Kaizen, Porirua Library, and Te Rauparaha Arena and Aquatic Centre all closed as a result of the burst water main.

A water tank was ordered for affected residents.

In the following hours, Tiaki Wai confirmed the outages had been contained to numbers 1-16 on Champion Street and all of Mepham Place.

World.title: Auckland Airport enters next phase of international terminal redevelopment
World.content:
Auckland Airport is moving into the next phase of its international terminal redevelopment, with retail and duty-free areas being refurbished for departing and arriving travellers.

The airport said the retail upgrade is its most significant airside refurbishment in a decade.

Work is underway on duty-free areas at international departures and arrivals, including two stores near departure gates.

The airport said the refurbished areas will have new layouts and a wider range of products, with beauty and fragrance at the centre of the changes.

Auckland Airport Chief Commercial Officer Mark Thomson said the changes are aimed at giving travellers a more engaging experience and greater choice.

"This is a deliberate move to strengthen our retail mix, provide an enhanced customer proposition, and modernise the space."

The redevelopment will also include new standalone retail stores, while the airport said further improvements to food and beverage areas are planned later this year.

Two standalone stores due to open later this year are skincare and bodycare brand Aesop and French fragrance brand Le Labo.

Some of the refurbished duty-free areas have already reopened, with the remaining retail refurbishment expected to be completed by December.

The airport said the overall footprint of its duty-free area will not increase as part of the redevelopment.

The international terminal transformation has been underway since January, with the work being carried out in stages while the terminal remains operational.

World.title: Nurse who cared for student who died at mental health unit can be named
World.content:
A name suppression order for one of the nurses responsible for the care of a 21-year-old student who died by suicide at a mental health ward has lapsed.

Erica Hume died in May 2014 at Palmerston North Hospital, a death Coroner Matthew Bates ruled was preventable and could have been avoided if staff had correctly followed policies and procedures.

He also found staff were under pressure due to the high number of patients and that the ward's physical environment wasn't fit for purpose. A replacement ward opened last year.

During an inquest into the death in 2022, temporary name suppression orders covered healthcare workers. When the coroner's ruling was released in June these orders lifted, except for one covering registered nurse Donna Jo-Anne Jones.

She was granted temporary suppression to allow her to consider an appeal against the coroner's ruling against her application for suppression.

She had until 31 July to do this, but the Coroner's Court and the High Court have confirmed no application was received.

Erica Hume's parents, Carey and Owen, said they were pleased to see the order lapse.

"Open justice does require people to be named and applications for a permanent non-disclosure order should be declined if there is truly to be embedded change in mental healthcare within New Zealand," they told RNZ in a statement.

Erica's father Owen Hume at his daughter's inquest. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Nurse's role among widespread systemic failures - coroner

Coroner Bates' ruling declining Jones' application for suppression said she cited interests of justice and personal privacy in arguing her name should remain secret. The coroner has ruled the specifics of her argument are suppressed.

Jones, who could not be contacted, managed Erica Hume's admission to the Palmerston North Hospital mental health ward, known as ward 21, on 6 May 2014 and nursed her that evening. Erica Hume died the next day.

The coroner found that despite Erica Hume's care worker giving a "detailed and diligent verbal handover", Jones did not take on board the heightened risk of suicide.

She also failed to adequately review admission information in Erica Hume's clinical file and record that information on admission documentation.

"These failures meant that from the time of admission to ward 21, Erica's heightened risk of suicide... went either unrecognised on the ward or, at the very least, the severity of her risk was not appreciated."

Coroner Matthew Bates at Erica Hume's inquest. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Coroner Bates said this affected the care Erica Hume received, including the levels of observation she was under, and the following shift wasn't fully appraised of the situation.

The coroner said Jones believed she did the best she could in the time available, writing in Erica Hume's file: "Admission paperwork to complete. Due to ward activity, unable to do."

Jones did not alone bear responsibility for Erica Hume's death and no individual was singled out for criticism in his findings, the coroner said.

"The role she played occurred in the context of widespread systemic failings and resourcing shortfalls at ward 21, including prolonged staff shortages."

Jones has been a registered nurse for almost 20 years and still works at Palmerston North Hospital.

Public interest in naming - Hume family

Carey and Owen Hume said after Erica's death they encountered a hospital system "embedded with non disclosure" and a "deep-seated expectation of non accountability".

"It is our opinion that accountability is a major factor in the examination of the care of Erica, and this includes the actions or inactions of all parties, staff and management.

"It is also our opinion that the purpose of having an inquest is to determine what happened and try to ensure that there is no repeat of the circumstances that allowed it to happen.

"This means, too, that individual as well as collective responsibility and accountability must occur."

Erica Hume in her Year 12 ball dress, taken several years before she died by suicide at Palmerston North Hospital aged 21. RNZ / Supplied

Carey and Owen Hume said for too long it was assumed healthcare workers would receive name suppression because it would harm their therapeutic relationship with patients, which was a a poor excuse.

"We firmly believe patients and families have the right to informed consent and knowledge of whom they are entrusting their care to," they said.

There was public interest in naming Jones and her not seeking to appeal against the coroner's ruling could be a sign she was taking responsibility for her role in what happened, which they said wasn't minor.

World.title: 38 dead after 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes off coast of Indonesia
World.content:
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck eastern Indonesia on Saturday killed at least 38 people, a disaster management official said, revising an earlier toll.

"Thirty-eight people have been confirmed dead, two were seriously injured, 11 sustained minor injuries, and approximately 2000 people have evacuated on their own," National Disaster Mitigation Agency chief Suharyanto told a news conference.

Dozens of aftershocks struck off eastern Indonesia after the main quake.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 metre were recorded in several areas of the Southeast Asian nation after the early morning tremor. The tsunami warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Rescuers around the port town of Maumere found 20 dead, six injured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, head of the city's rescue agency. Maumere is the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in the east of Indonesia's vast archipelago.

Teams were yet to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicentre, and communications signals there had been affected, Fathur told Reuters. Attempts to reach Nagekeo by car were blocked by landslides, while another team was attempting to go by ferry, he said.

Rescuers working amid the rubble of a damaged building after an earthquake in Maumere, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP PHOTO / INDONESIA'S NATIONAL SEARCH AND RESCUE AGENCY (BASARNAS)

About 2000 residents in Nagekeo evacuated, and damage was reported to a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities, national disaster mitigation agency BNPB said. Authorities also reported traffic congestion and power outages affecting parts of the regency, it said.

The governor of East Nusa Tenggara Province, Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, told a press conference at least five people died from collapsing rubble as they slept.

The BNPB, which put the quake's toll at one dead and four injured, said it was still gathering data.

"I have never felt an earthquake this big," Yulian Juita Ekalia, who lives in Ruteng city more than 100km west of the epicentre, told AFP by telephone.

"It felt like we were on a trampoline; it was really scary," said the 37-year-old university lecturer, who jolted awake at around 5:30am local time.

"As I rushed to get outside, everything in the house fell down: the television, my son's trophies, the dish racks, suitcases on top of the wardrobes. When I got outside, my son and neighbours were already there, screaming in fear."

Parts of a building collapsed into dust and rubble as people screamed and ran in the street, a video on Facebook, verified by Reuters as being at a port in Maumere, showed.

"The quake was massive, the shock was so strong, we were resting at home with family," said Nona, a 51-year-old resident of Talibura, a village in East Nusa Tenggara. "There were 13 of us inside the house and we all ran to save ourselves."

Strong shaking was felt across East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara and parts of South Sulawesi, and residents in several areas reported shaking lasting about one minute, BNPB said in a statement.

Damaged houses in Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP / Selo

"Most of the people felt the shock and scattered out of their homes," it said.

A hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province was moving patients outside, Kompas TV footage showed, and Kompas.com reported at least one landslide.

Indonesian geophysics agency BMKG recorded the first quake at 4:58am at a depth of 15 km, followed by several aftershocks.

In 1992 the same area was hit by a magnitude-7.5 quake, causing extensive destruction at that time, the agency said.

No threat to NZ

There was no tsunami threat to New Zealand or Australia following the quake.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade was monitoring the situation and working with Indonesian authorities to assess the earthquake's impact, an MFAT spokesperson said.

There are 277 people from New Zealand registered on SafeTravel as being in Indonesia and 22 in Timor-Leste.

A damaged buildingin Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP / Selo

MFAT was not aware of any New Zealanders who had requested assistance, the spokesperson said.

New Zealanders who require urgent consular assistance can contact the 24/7 consular emergency line on +64 99 20 20 20 or 0800 30 10 30.

Those in the affected areas should follow the advice of local authorities at all times. New Zealanders should also register on SafeTravel and, when they are able, let their family and friends in NZ know that they are safe, MFAT said.

World.title: Best-selling writer Meg Mason loved growing up Exclusive Brethren, but it left her feeling 'permanently othered'
World.content: "Everybody thinks that you race out and do all the things that you weren't allowed to do, but that's not true because you've had this fear ingrained in you that, you know, drinking is evil and horoscopes are evil… I'm 48, and I could not read a horoscope with a gun to my head. I don't even know what star sign I am," Mason tells RNZ's Saturday Morning .

World.title: MPs shocked by fatal Aranui dog attack
World.content:
The local MP says he was distressed to hear that a young child had died after a dog attack in the Christchurch suburb of Aranui.

Police found the child in a critical condition after being called to a house on Basingstoke Street just before 5pm on Friday. They later died at the scene.

MP for the Christchurch East electorate, Reuben Davidson, said it was a tragedy for the family and the wider community.

Local Burwood Ward councillor Kelly Barber said his first thoughts were with the child's family.

"It's a very sad situation, and my first thoughts were with the family and how devastated they must be at the loss of their child. I also hope there is something we can learn from the ongoing police investigation that reduces the likelihood of this ever happening again," he said.

Police investigators have left the scene.

The dog, which lived at the house, was removed by Animal Control, and police were speaking with the residents and providing support.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition," Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said.

Basingstoke Street, Christchurch, 15 August. Tim Brown / RNZ

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

St John said two ambulances, two rapid response units and one operations manager attended.

Govt weighs stronger dog control penalties, greater council powers

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said the Government was reviewing the Dog Control Act to ensure councils had the tools to manage dangerous dogs and protect communities.

"The news of this dog attack is devastating, and my thoughts are with the child's family, and everyone affected," he said.

"Every New Zealander should be able to feel safe in their community and not fear being attacked by a dangerous and uncontrolled dog."

Watts said stronger penalties and greater powers for council officers were among the options being considered as part of the review.

He said the Government had also released updated Dog Control and Enforcement Guidelines, giving councils clearer and more consistent guidance under the current framework.

Officials were working with councils, animal control officers and other stakeholders to identify further changes that might be needed, he said.

World.title: Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan
World.content:
Massimo De Lutiis has enjoyed a dream debut for Australia, as the 1,000th Wallaby scored a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

De Lutiis came on in the 50th minute of the Test match in Townsville with the match delicately poised at 21-17, the half-time score.

But the introduction of the hulking 22-year-old began the start of Australia's dominance in the Test match, as fellow prop Angus Bell scored the first of five second-half tries.

De Lutiis, with the descendants of the very first Wallaby Patrick Carew in attendance, scored minutes later to send his teammates, and the crowd, into a frenzy.

"One thousand is awesome. But just to be a Wallaby in general is crazy to me. It's a dream come true," De Lutiis told the Nine Network post-match.

"When I scored, I was just over the moon. I couldn't believe it."

After a difficult first half, the Wallabies improved in attack and defence to earn the win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the impressive scoreline, the Wallabies were tested in the opening 50 minutes, with the Japanese taking the lead late in the first half.

At three tries apiece after 40 minutes, the Brave Blossoms had every right to believe a maiden win over the Wallabies was there for the taking.

But Australia showed the polish which eluded them in the first half, and the first Test in Osaka last weekend.

New coach Les Kiss, in his second match in charge, provided the right team talk at half-time to wrestle momentum from Japan.

"We got challenged by Les [Kiss] at half-time," captain Harry Wilson told the Nine Network.

"A team like Japan, if you're not up for it, they really make you pay.

"I was really proud of the group in the second half. We stepped it up and put on a great performance."

The win is Australia's third in a row, the first time the Wallabies have strung together a trio of triumphs since 2024.

The challenge for Australia gets harder, with two Tests in Argentina followed by one Test against South Africa, and two Bledisloe Cup matches against the All Blacks.

World.title: Live: Hawks rattled by manic Magpies pressure as Dees dominate Port in first half
World.content:
Collingwood and Melbourne race out to early leads in their respective clashes against Hawthorn and Port Adelaide.

Earlier on Saturday, St Kilda kept its wildcard hopes alive with a convincing 14.10 (94) to 6.9 (45) win at the MCG.

Geelong came back from a 38-point deficit to defeat North Melbourne 19.11 (125) to 17.8 (110) at Docklands Stadium as the Kangaroos lost Harry Sheezel to a cheek injury.

Elsewhere, Brisbane kicked away in the second half to claim a 14.11 (95) to 6.17 (53) win over Gold Coast in the latest edition of the Q-Clash at the Gabba.

World.title: Cyclist, 19, dies during Volta a Portugal after collision with vehicle
World.content:
A 19-year-old British cyclist has been killed in an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Welsh rider Finlay Tarling died after "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle", Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said in a statement.

An investigation is underway, according to local authorities.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

He was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8-kilometre route from Melgaco to Fafe.

Riders are seen in Fafe, Portugal, reacting to the news that Finlay Tarling had died. (Getty Images: Miguel Lemos/NurPhoto)

In a statement, NSN said the team was heartbroken to announce Tarling's passing.

"Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

The intrinsic failings and risks of cycling laid bare with another premature death Cycling has lost another rider due to a downhill crash, with teenager Muriel Furrer killed on a descent at the World Championships in Zurich. So where does the responsibility lie?

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation also expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president António José Seguro said that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh, at this tragic time."

World.title: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets
World.content:
Australia has closed day three of the first Test against Bangladesh on 4-161, still 67 runs behind the tourists on another chastening day in Darwin.

Alex Carey (19) and Cameron Green (43) are the not out batters, combining for a valuable 39-run partnership late in the day that will prove crucial for Australia's chances of saving, or perhaps even winning the Test.

Australia will back itself to make Bangladesh bat again but, on an increasingly placid pitch, will have to bat very well to set a challenging target to the tourists, a scenario almost inconceivable for supporters of the world's number one side prior to the match getting underway.

With Bangladesh resuming on 6-351, Australia once again struggled to make inroads, extending their already gruelling labours in the field.

Josh Hazlewood thought he had made the breakthrough when umpire Richard Illingworth fired out Mehidy Hasan LBW, only for the DRS to show the ball was missing the leg stump.

The veteran quick was frustrated then, but soon was celebrating when Hasan Mahmud was trapped bang in front to depart for 14.

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood then claimed another, having Taijul Islam caught sharply by Cam Green, whose self-preservation instincts came to the fore to stop the ball flying into his face at gully.

If those two wickets had Australia thinking they'd soon be batting, the discipline of the Bangladeshi batters made sure they had to stay out even longer, coupled with a shocking drop from Steve Smith.

Taskin Ahmed top edged a pull shot out to Smith, who settled under the ball and let it through his finger tips.

A few balls later, Travis Head dropped a far harder chance, racing around from close to the wicket as Bangladesh reached 8-417 at lunch.

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

The mounting frustration eased somewhat by two more Hazlewood wickets, as he claimed Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Ebadot Hossain, both caught behind, to secure a 14th Test five-fa and his 300th Test wicket, becoming the ninth Australian to reach that particular milestone.

Australia needed a good start, but under-pressure home-town favourite Jake Weatherald departed second over for a duck, chopping on after playing with an angled bat to Hasan Mahmud.

Failing to learn from his first innings dismissal and that of his opening partner, Travis Head followed in near identical fashion to leave Australia 2-37 and in desperate trouble.

Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith came to the crease and both survived big Bangladeshi appeals, with Smith forced to review a caught behind decision when he was on three, the replay showing that he hit the ground with his bat instead of the ball.

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

That pair looked set, with Labuschagne seemingly playing with am encouragingly positive intent that was desperately lacking in his first innings effort.

However, the Queenslander was next to depart, playing all around a Taijul Islam fuller ball and yorking himself against the spinner to be out for 31.

Smith and Cameron Green rebuilt with a patient and untroubled 49-run partnership on an increasingly docile pitch, right up until Smith flat-batted a return catch to Bangladesh's other spinner, Mehidy Hasan for 44.

Australia still trailed by over 100 runs at that stage, with Alex Carey joining Green, who incredibly survived an inside edge that clipped his leg stump without dislodging the bail early in the evening session.

They batted out the remainder of the day without too much alarm, but know they will have to fight just as hard to save this Test match over the next two days.

World.title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
World.content:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives
World.content:
Kookaburras midfielder Liam Henderson has the attitude of a winner.

It is a confidence that comes with being part of a team used to sustained excellence, backed by a growing reputation as one of hockey's global rising stars.

And in his second year on the national team, the 22-year-old is ready to deliver at the World Cup which begins this weekend.

"We think we can win it. And if other teams don't think we can, we'll just prove them wrong," he told ABC Sport from the team's base in Belgium.

Liam Henderson (right) is heading to his first World Cup. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world, and won the last of their three World Cup titles in 2014.

Recent FIH Pro League victories over the top two ranked teams, Belgium and Netherlands, mean Henderson's confidence is justified.

"Everyone brings their natural game. We're a force to be reckoned with," he said.

"The last two games we played against the two world's best, we had two wins and two losses. We can beat them. And if it's our day, anything can happen."

The Kookaburras have won the World Cup three times. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The team's last major tournament was the Paris 2024 Olympics, which ended in an uncharacteristic quarter-final exit.

There has been significant change since then with a new coach, Mark Hager, and the retirements of some of their longest serving players including Eddie Ockenden, Aran Zalewski, and Andrew Charter.

But a hallmark of the Kookaburras throughout their history has been a constant ability to regenerate and maintain their position amongst the world's top teams.

"As a hockey community, we're always watching our national teams. And when you watch them, something you aspire to do is just be in that team," Henderson said.

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"And once you're there, I think every chance you get, you just want to work as hard as possible.

"I think another piece of that is the group that we have at the moment are all so close.

"We're such good mates, all of us, and such a welcoming team that you just want to play for each other. It's something you really want to be a part of."

Hockeyroos to rise up

The men's tournament will be played in Wavre, just outside of Brussels, played concurrently with the women's event in Amstelveen, Netherlands.

That is where the Hockeyroos are based, led by the most experienced player in the team, co-captain Kaitlin Nobbs, heading to her third World Cup.

She is part of one of the sport's most illustrious dynasties, with both parents having represented Australia, alongside her grandmother, aunty, and uncle — the Kookaburras coach.

Kaitlin Nobbs is playing at her third World Cup. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"Coming into this one it marks the 40th anniversary from when my mum went to a World Cup as well representing the Hockeyroos," Nobbs told ABC Sport.

"So looking at the past and reflecting and seeing where we've come from, where the Hockeyroos have come from until now, it means the world to be able to go out and represent the team and captain them."

Her dad, Michael Nobbs, died earlier this year, and has provided her with extra motivation to excel.

"I think he would be so chuffed that I'm playing and enjoying the game and trying to take the most out of it that I can," she said.

"He loved hockey more than anyone and loved watching me play. So I'm sure he'll be watching and following along from wherever he is."

The Hockeyroos are ranked eighth in the world, and after winning the last of their three Olympic golds in 2000, have not managed to reach those heights again, although bronze at the 2022 World Cup was a highlight.

Katrina Powell took over as coach just before the Tokyo Olympics in the wake of systemic cultural issues in the women's program, and after stepping down last year, she was replaced by former South Africa men's international Rhett Halkett.

The Hockeyroos have had a period of change over the past two years. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"I think we are more than capable of playing in the finals for a medal," Nobbs said.

"Rhett comes from a bit of a European background, so we've changed up how we've played in the past year.

"This year in itself has been enough stress for the next four years or the last four years because we've had to play Pro League, qualify for this World Cup, change our structure, change our way of play.

The Hockeyroos celebrate a penalty shootout win over the Netherlands, to secure a spot in next year's FIH Pro League. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"So it has been a crazy journey, but I think all of those things give you experience and evidence leading into big tournaments like this that you can lean on."

Growing the game

The interest in hockey is at a different level in Europe, particularly in Belgium and the Netherlands, and it is something Henderson is embracing.

"Just walking around the streets, you're seeing billboards, you're seeing [players] on bus stops," Henderson said.

"I think the general population know more about the game."

Henderson has also started to make a name for himself in India, another hockey hotbed, after fetching the highest price at the Hockey India League auction last year — around $71,500.

While not in the same ballpark as the IPL, it is a lucrative league for Australians, who usually juggle studying or work alongside playing.

"I was actually in the gym with a few of my teammates when [the auction] was going down," Henderson said.

"It was more just shock. I'd only played 11 international games at that stage. And I think just showed potentially what people think I can do.

"The team obviously were very successful, we won a tournament. It was such a valuable experience for me. You can't put a price tag on that."

Henderson and Nobbs also play in Australia's domestic league, Hockey One, and hope to see its continued growth.

"It's finally a competition that gets talked about, I think, internationally and really good players from abroad wanting to come over and be part of that competition," Nobbs said.

"We obviously compete with a lot of sports in Australia, cricket, soccer, netball, everything.

"So to have a product like that growing and something exciting that young kids can come and watch is definitely a good thing."

World.title: What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
World.content:
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.

But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.

For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.

But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.

By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.

Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.

"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.

Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.

"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.

For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation; it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals, the Giants.

For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.

Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.

Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.

While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.

Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.

McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.

Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.

"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."

In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.

All good coaches evolve. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.

The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.

In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.

There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.

But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.

Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.

This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.

Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.

"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.

ABC AFL Daily podcast Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."

The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hit-outs and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.

Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.

"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.

It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.

"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.

"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.

"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."

Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.

The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.

Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in the wake of the win, the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.

"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.

"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."

Suns keen to rise in 2027

In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.

"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.

"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."

Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.

Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.

Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.

These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.

The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.

Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.
